title: Star Chart Location Setup: Sky App Coordinates
description: Set up any star chart or planetarium app with your exact coordinates using Star Chart Location Setup — latitude is destiny for the night sky. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, from New York (latitude 40.758°) Polaris sits 40.8 degrees above the northern horizon and the celestial equator culminates 49.2 degrees up in the south — your latitude writes your sky.
quick_answer: Star Chart Location Setup gives you the precise latitude and longitude your telescope apps, planetarium software and night-sky charts need to draw YOUR sky. Find or confirm your coordinates here, enter them in the app, and the chart's horizon, pole and planet positions finally match the sky above your garden.
steps_intro: A star chart is only as good as the location it is set for:

body.t: Stellarium, SkySafari and their kin all ask for a location before anything else. Supply coordinates, not just a town — the
finds them for any observing site.
Driving to darker skies changes your latitude little and your longitude's clock a lot — update the app at the site and the chart's timing snaps back to truth.
Polar alignment, target rise times and twilight depth all compute from the site's coordinates. Wrong farm, wrong night.
Apps guess from networks and get fields wrong by kilometres. Verify the stored location against a known pair here.

examples.label: Example · Latitude is the sky's tilt

body.t: Polaris's altitude equals your latitude (40.8° from New York, ~51.5° from London, near the horizon at the equator). No other single number rearranges a star chart more — which is why apps ask for it first.

examples.label: Example · Longitude is the sky's clock

body.t: Two observers on the same latitude see the same sky at different clock times — longitude shifts when stars culminate. A chart set to your town but timed for the meridian's town drifts visibly.

popular_table.note: Altitude/elevation above sea level barely moves a star chart — it matters for horizon dip and refraction at the extremes, not for finding your sky. Coordinates and clock are the whole game.

faq: How precise must my coordinates be?

Town-level precision draws a chart indistinguishable to the eye. Arc-minute precision matters for telescope GoTo pointing and occultation timing — take the pair from a map click at your exact observing spot for those.
The app shows a different sky than I see.
Check in order: location, then time zone, then the device clock. Nine times in ten the stored location is a stale auto-guess from another town.
Everything mirrors: the south celestial pole is the pivot, Polaris vanishes, and latitude's sign does the tilting. The setup is the same — the sky is not.
Why does the app want elevation too?
For horizon and refraction niceties and satellite passes — provide it if asked, but know coordinates and time carry the chart.
Charts compute in UTC internally; a phone in the wrong DST state shifts the sky by an hour's rotation (15 degrees). Verify the clock when the chart looks rotated.
Can I plan for a future trip's sky?
Set the destination's coordinates and the trip's date — planetariums happily draw next month's sky over a place you have not reached yet.
They are brutally location-sensitive (a few kilometres change the pass) — site-exact coordinates, as this page insists, are the price of seeing one.
